Know your scope — and when to bring in a dietitian.

Topic 01 — Role of Sports Nutrition Professionals

Where Your Scope Ends

Sports Nutrition Coach
S&C coach acting as nutrition coach → basic education + general guidance (e.g. "healthy snack ideas").
Sports Dietitian (RD/RDN)
Individualized dietary advice + medical nutrition therapy → complex/clinical cases.
All sports nutrition professionals should answer basic questions — individualized advice requires referral.
Topic 01 — Role of Sports Nutrition Professionals

The CSSD Credential

  • Role Counsels individuals/teams on daily nutrition for performance + health
  • Role Translates evidence → practical sports nutrition recommendations
  • Role Tracks/documents nutrition outcomes for coaches, staff, families
  • Task Assesses body composition, energy needs, fluid/electrolyte balance
  • Task Evaluates supplements + ergogenic aids using evidence-based analysis
  • Task Supports disordered eating interventions + monitoring
Higher-level positions: sports dietitian with master's degree, PhD, or both.
Topic 01 — Role of Sports Nutrition Professionals

When to Refer

Medical Conditions
Eating disorders, nutrient deficiencies, disease states (e.g. diabetes) → team physician + sports dietitian.
Legal Scope
State licensure laws govern who can provide individualized nutrition counseling. Unlicensed advice = liability risk.
Athlete health info shared across staff → follow HIPAA guidelines (US).
Topic 01 — Role of Sports Nutrition Professionals

Key Takeaway

Answer basic questions. Refer complex cases to a sports dietitian (RD/RDN) or team physician — know your scope, know your state's licensure laws.

Topic 02

Standard
Nutrition
Guidelines

MyPlate, DRIs, and the nutrients athletes fall short on.

Source: myplate.gov
Topic 02 — Standard Nutrition Guidelines

The MyPlate Framework

MyPlate (USDA)
5 food groups via mealtime visual → fruits, vegetables, grains, protein, dairy. Starting point to evaluate an athlete's diet.
Performance Enhancing Plate
CPSDA version for hard training days → 1/2 plate whole grains, 1/4 fruits/vegetables, 1/4 protein.
Excluding a food group → risk gaps (e.g. no dairy → ↓ calcium/vitamin D). Work with a sports dietitian to find replacements.
Topic 02 — Standard Nutrition Guidelines

Nutrients to Watch

  • Oils Not a food group → source of MUFA/PUFA + vitamin E
  • Added sugars Limit for general population; exception = athlete hydration beverages
  • Saturated fat Solid at room temp (butter, milk fat) → limit, favor unsaturated oils
  • Sodium ≤2,300 mg/day general population; endurance/heavy-sweat athletes may need more
  • Alcohol Calories, few nutrients → moderation only, legal drinking age
MyPlate = starting point, not a fixed prescription — adjust to activity level.
Topic 02 — Standard Nutrition Guidelines

Dietary Reference Intakes

  • RDA Meets needs of ~97–98% healthy people in a life stage/sex → plans adequate diets
  • AI Used when an RDA can't be established
  • UL Max intake with no adverse effects — from food + water + supplements combined
  • EAR Meets needs of half the healthy population in a life stage/sex
Sports dietitians average multiple days of intake — day-to-day variation is high, especially for micronutrients.
Topic 02 — Standard Nutrition Guidelines

Nutrients of Public Health Concern

Under-Consumed (All Adults)
Fiber, vitamin D, calcium, potassium. >90% women / 97% men miss fiber targets.
Iron — Female Athletes
Iron-deficient anemia 5–7× more common vs. male athletes. Sources: shellfish, fortified cereals, dark leafy greens, soybeans, red meat, poultry.
Potassium/calcium/vitamin D sources: potatoes, dairy, fortified beverages, fatty fish.
Topic 02 — Standard Nutrition Guidelines

Key Takeaway

MyPlate + DRIs guide general nutrition — but adjust for activity level, and flag fiber, vitamin D, calcium, potassium, and iron (especially in female athletes) as common gaps.

Topic 03

Macronutrients

The three nutrient classes the body needs in bulk.

Topic 03 — Macronutrients

What Is a Macronutrient?

A nutrient required in significant amounts in the diet.
1
Protein
Structural & functional component of every cell
2
Carbohydrate
Primary energy source — not an essential nutrient
3
Fat
Triglycerides — the body's main lipid form
Topic 04

Protein

Amino acids, quality, and how much athletes really need.

Topic 04 — Protein

The Body's Building Block

Primary structural + functional component of every cell.
  • Growth Builds + repairs cells and tissue
  • Enzymes Catalyze biochemical reactions
  • Transport Carries molecules through the blood
  • Hormones Regulate physiological processes
Photo: Mark DeYoung / Unsplash
Topic 04 — Protein

Essential vs. Nonessential

Essential (9)
Body can't manufacture → must come from diet.
Nonessential (4)
Synthesized by the body → not required in diet.
Conditionally Essential (7)
Become essential during illness/stress.
Amino acids → peptide bonds → dipeptide (2) → polypeptide (many) → proteins.
AI-generated image
Topic 04 — Protein

Protein Quality

Animal Sources
Eggs, dairy, meat, fish, poultry → all 9 EAAs. Highly digestible.
Plant Sources
Soy, quinoa, buckwheat → only plant proteins with all 9 EAAs. Vary plant foods across the day to cover gaps.
PDCAAS = digestibility + EAA content — doesn't account for antinutritional factors that ↓ bioavailability (e.g. Maillard browning).
Topic 04 — Protein

How Much Protein?

  • RDA 0.8 g/kg/day — adults 19+, based on nitrogen balance studies
  • AMDR 10–35% of total calories for adults
  • Inverse rule ↓ calorie intake → ↑ protein needs as % of calories
Sports dietitians set protein first, then add carbs/fat to meet total calorie needs.
Topic 04 — Protein

Protein & Health

Bone Health
50% of bone volume, 33% of bone mass. Supports bone when paired with adequate calcium.
Weight Management
↑ satiety (dose-dependent) + highest thermic effect of feeding + spares muscle during calorie restriction.
Topic 04 — Protein

Athlete Targets

Endurance Athletes
1.2–2.0 g/kg/day
Muscle Building/Maintenance
1.4–2.0 g/kg/day
Reduced-calorie diets → may need more protein to preserve muscle tissue.
Topic 04 — Protein

Protein Timing

  • Dose 20–40g high-quality protein every 3–4 hours
  • Workout window ~0.4–0.5 g/kg lean body mass, pre + post within 4–6 hrs of each other
  • Priority Total daily intake > precise timing for muscle growth
Muscle stays sensitive to protein for ≥24 hours post-resistance training.
Topic 04 — Protein

Is More Protein Safe?

Intakes up to 2.8 g/kg/day showed no impaired renal function in athletes (7-day diet record study).
  • Excess Nitrogen excreted as urea; ketoacids → energy, gluconeogenesis, or fat storage
  • Watch for Very high intake may crowd out carb/fat-rich foods and their nutrients
Topic 04 — Protein

Key Takeaway

RDA = 0.8 g/kg minimum. Athletes need 1.2–2.0 g/kg — spread across the day in 20–40g doses. Set protein first, then build carbs/fat around it.

Topic 05

Carbohydrate

Fuel classification, glycogen, and the GI/GL toolkit.

Topic 05 — Carbohydrate

Carbohydrate's Role

Primary energy source — but not an essential nutrient.
  • Composition Carbon, hydrogen, oxygen
  • Not essential Body can make glucose from amino acids via gluconeogenesis
  • Classified by Number of sugar units → mono-/di-/polysaccharides
Photo: Abhishek Hajare / Unsplash
Topic 05 — Carbohydrate

The Three Classes

Monosaccharides
Glucose, fructose, galactose. Glucose = primary energy substrate; fructose ↓ insulin response.
Disaccharides
Sucrose (glucose+fructose), lactose (glucose+galactose), maltose (glucose+glucose).
Polysaccharides
Starch, fiber, glycogen — up to thousands of glucose units.
Topic 05 — Carbohydrate

Glycogen Storage

~15 g glycogen / kg body weight — stored in muscle + liver.
  • Muscle ~3/4 of the body's glycogen stores
  • Liver ~1/4 of the body's glycogen stores
  • Glycogenesis Process of converting glucose → glycogen
Topic 05 — Carbohydrate

Glycemic Index (GI)

GI = (blood glucose response ÷ reference food response) × 100
  • Reference White bread/glucose = GI of 100
  • Low-GI Slower digestion → smaller blood glucose/insulin rise
  • Application Low-GI base diet; high-GI foods around training for fast fuel + glycogen refill
GI values shift with ripeness, processing, and meal composition — limits precision.
Topic 05 — Carbohydrate

Glycemic Load (GL)

GL = (GI × grams carbohydrate per serving) ÷ 100
Accounts for portion size → more realistic gauge of glycemic response than GI alone.
  • Higher GL Greater blood sugar/insulin rise
  • Low-GI/GL diets Linked to lower fasting insulin + inflammatory markers
Topic 05 — Carbohydrate

Fiber

DRI
Women: 21–25 g/day. Men: 30–38 g/day (varies by age).
Sources
Fruits, vegetables, nuts, seeds, legumes, whole grains.
Low fiber intake ↔ constipation, heart disease, colon cancer, type 2 diabetes risk.
Topic 05 — Carbohydrate

Allergies vs. Sensitivities

Food Allergy
Immune response, reproducible on exposure. Range: rash → anaphylaxis. Top 8 US allergens: milk, wheat, eggs, tree nuts, peanut, fish, shellfish, soy.
Food Sensitivity
Nonimmune reaction (metabolic/toxic/pharmacologic). ~25% self-reported prevalence. Lactose = most common (~65%).
Celiac disease = immune response to gluten (wheat, rye, barley). Refer to a registered dietitian for elimination/reintroduction plans.
Topic 05 — Carbohydrate

Key Takeaway

Carbs fuel training. Prioritize whole-food polysaccharides + fiber, use GI/GL strategically around exercise, and screen for allergies/intolerances before big dietary changes.

Topic 06

Fat

Fatty acid types, cholesterol, and fat as fuel.

Topic 06 — Fat

Fat's Energy Density

Lipid = broader term. Fat (this chapter) = triglycerides — glycerol + 3 fatty acids.
  • Composition Carbon, hydrogen, oxygen — more C/H relative to O than carbs
  • Energy ~9 kcal/g vs. ~4 kcal/g for carbohydrate/protein
  • Function Drives flavor, aroma, texture of food
Photo: Sorin Gheorghita / Unsplash
Topic 06 — Fat

Fatty Acid Types

Saturated
No double bonds. Body can synthesize → no dietary requirement.
Monounsaturated
One double bond. Olive, peanut, canola oils.
Polyunsaturated
2+ double bonds. Soy, corn, sunflower, safflower oils. Includes essential omega-3/omega-6.
Topic 06 — Fat

Omega-6 vs. Omega-3

Omega-6
Abundant in food supply — soybean, corn, safflower oil.
Omega-3
Fatty fish (salmon, herring, halibut, trout, mackerel) → EPA/DHA. ↓ triglycerides, modest ↓ blood pressure.
ALA (flaxseed, walnuts, soybean/canola oil) converts to EPA/DHA — inefficiently: ~5% → EPA, <0.5% → DHA.
Topic 06 — Fat

Fat's Functions

  • Energy storage Primarily adipose tissue; some in skeletal muscle (aerobically trained athletes)
  • Insulation Protects organs
  • Hormones Regulates hormone production
  • Vitamin transport Carries + stores fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, K
Topic 06 — Fat

Cholesterol

Functions
Structural component of cell membranes. Makes bile salts, vitamin D, sex hormones, cortisol.
LDL/VLDL vs. HDL
High LDL/VLDL → atherogenic, ↑ heart disease risk. High HDL = protective (not a therapy target).
High saturated/trans fat, weight gain → ↑ LDL. High carbohydrate intake → ↑ VLDL.
Topic 06 — Fat

Cholesterol Targets

  • LDL <100 optimal · 100–159 near optimal/borderline · 160–189 high · ≥190 very high
  • Total <200 desirable · 200–239 borderline high · ≥240 high
  • HDL <40 low · ≥60 high
Limit saturated fat to <10% of total calories — replace with unsaturated, especially polyunsaturated.
Topic 06 — Fat

Fat & Performance

Fat stores = vast fuel reserve. 160 lb runner @ 4% body fat → ~22,400 kcal stored in fat tissue.
  • Rest/low intensity High % of energy from fat oxidation
  • ↑ Exercise intensity Gradual shift fat → carbohydrate as preferred fuel
  • Aerobic training ↑ muscle's capacity to use fatty acids
Topic 06 — Fat

Fat & Alcohol Guidelines

  • Saturated fat <10% of total calories → replace with unsaturated (esp. polyunsaturated)
  • Alcohol Moderation — ≤1 drink/day women, ≤2 drinks/day men, legal age only
  • Post-exercise Avoid alcohol → reduces muscle protein synthesis
Pregnant: avoid alcohol entirely. Breastfeeding: consult healthcare provider.
Topic 06 — Fat

Key Takeaway

Prioritize unsaturated fats + essential omega-3s, keep saturated fat <10% of calories — fat is the body's largest fuel reserve, and trained athletes tap it more efficiently.

Topic 07

Vitamins

Water-soluble vs. fat-soluble — and where toxicity risk hides.

Topic 07 — Vitamins

What Is a Vitamin?

Organic substances needed in very small amounts for specific metabolic functions.
  • Role Mostly act as coenzymes → facilitate biochemical reactions
  • Example B vitamins help the body make energy from carbohydrate metabolism
  • Classes 13 vitamins total, split into water-soluble and fat-soluble
Photo: Madara / Unsplash
Topic 07 — Vitamins

Water- vs. Fat-Soluble

Water-Soluble
B vitamins + vitamin C. Travel in blood. Not stored (except B12 → liver, years). Excess excreted in urine.
Fat-Soluble
Vitamins A, D, E, K. Carried by fat in blood, stored in fat tissue. Excess can accumulate → toxicity risk.
Topic 07 — Vitamins

Fat-Soluble At a Glance

  • A Vision, skin, tissue, mucous membrane health
  • D Calcium absorption, bone mass, prevents bone loss
  • E Antioxidant, immune function, metabolism
  • K Blood clotting, tissue + bone health
Topic 07 — Vitamins

Water-Soluble At a Glance

  • C Cell development, wound healing, antioxidant, iron absorption
  • B1/B2/Niacin Coenzymes for carb/protein/fat metabolism + nervous system function
  • B6/Folate/B12 Protein metabolism, red blood cell formation, nervous system
  • Biotin/B5 Fatty acid metabolism, growth & development
Topic 07 — Vitamins

Fat-Soluble Toxicity Risks

  • A Liver damage, intracranial pressure, nausea, coma — usually from supplements
  • D Heart arrhythmias, ↑ blood calcium → vessel/tissue calcification
  • E Anticoagulant effect → ↑ hemorrhagic stroke risk (esp. on blood thinners)
  • K Interferes with anticlotting meds (e.g. warfarin)
Water-soluble vitamins rarely cause toxicity — excess is excreted in urine.
Topic 07 — Vitamins

Antioxidants

Modify cell-signaling pathways + counteract oxidative stress from free radicals.
  • Free radicals Both beneficial and harmful — excess + low antioxidant intake → cell damage
  • Key vitamins Vitamin C, vitamin E, beta carotene (→ converts to vitamin A)
  • Damage target Cellular lipids, proteins, DNA
Topic 07 — Vitamins

Key Takeaway

Water-soluble vitamins (B-complex + C) need regular intake — they're not stored. Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) accumulate in fat tissue, so watch supplement doses to avoid toxicity.

Topic 08

Minerals

Iron and calcium — the two that deserve extra attention.

Topic 08 — Minerals

Minerals & Their Roles

Contribute to bone/teeth/nail structure, form enzymes, and drive metabolic functions.
  • Major minerals Calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, iron
  • Electrolytes Sodium, potassium, chloride
  • Athlete relevance Bone health, oxygen-carrying capacity, fluid/electrolyte balance
Photo: Dose Juice / Unsplash
Topic 08 — Minerals

Minerals At a Glance

  • Ca/P/Mg Bone/teeth structure, nerve + muscle function, enzyme activation
  • Fe/Zn/Cu Oxygen transport, enzyme systems, immune function + wound healing
  • Se/Cr/I Antioxidant defense, glucose metabolism, thyroid function
  • Mn/Mo Connective tissue development, DNA/RNA metabolism
Topic 08 — Minerals

Iron — Function & Deficiency

Essential for hemoglobin (oxygen transport) + myoglobin (oxygen to muscle).
  • 3 stages Depletion → marginal deficiency → anemia
  • At-risk Women of childbearing age, teen girls, distance runners, vegetarian/female athletes
  • Symptoms Fatigue, weakness, poor concentration, ↓ exercise capacity, hair loss
Topic 08 — Minerals

Heme vs. Nonheme Iron

Heme Iron
Animal foods (red meat, fish, poultry). ~15–35% absorbed. Not affected by other foods.
Nonheme Iron
Plant foods, fortified cereals. Only ~2–20% absorbed. Inhibited by phytic acid, tannins, calcium, polyphenols.
Boost absorption: pair with vitamin C-rich foods, or eat alongside heme iron (e.g. spinach + meat).
Topic 08 — Minerals

Iron Supplementation

  • Ferrous iron Highest bioavailability — most recommended form
  • Timing Empty stomach, ≥1 hr before meals, for max absorption
  • Avoid pairing with Whole grains, coffee, black tea, red wine, calcium, magnesium
Only a medical doctor or registered dietitian should recommend iron supplementation + dosing.
Topic 08 — Minerals

Calcium & Bone Health

Up to 90% of peak bone mineral density develops during late adolescence.
  • Shortfall Calcium pulled from bone to maintain blood levels → weakens bone over time
  • NHANES Just 15% of girls 9–13, <10% of women 14–18/51+ meet adequate calcium intake
  • Beyond bone Muscle contraction, nerve function, blood vessel + hormone/enzyme regulation
Topic 08 — Minerals

Nutrient vs. Caloric Density

Nutrient-Dense
Milk, vegetables, protein foods, grains → rich in vitamins/minerals/fiber relative to calories.
Calorie-Dense, Nutrient-Poor
Potato chips, desserts, candy → high calories, low nutrient value.
Topic 08 — Minerals

Key Takeaway

Iron and calcium deserve special attention in athletes — screen at-risk groups, pair nonheme iron with vitamin C, and prioritize nutrient-dense foods to hit bone and blood targets.

Topic 09

Fluid and
Electrolytes

Hydration assessment, sodium balance, and building an individualized plan.

Topic 09 — Fluid and Electrolytes

Water's Role

45–75% of body weight. Balance = intake (food/drinks/metabolic water) vs. output (sweat, urine, feces, expired air).
  • Functions Lubricant, shock absorber, building material, solvent
  • Also Temperature regulation, nutrient transport, waste removal, blood pressure
  • AI (Adequate Intake) Men 3.7 L/day · Women 2.7 L/day · Pregnant 3.0 L/day · Lactating 3.8 L/day
Photo: NutraSeller Manufacturing / Unsplash
Topic 09 — Fluid and Electrolytes

Dehydration Risk Factors

Even mild dehydration (2–3% body weight loss) impairs fatigue, motivation, strength, and power.
  • NFL linemen ~2.25 L/hr sweat loss (vs. ~1.4 L/hr backs/receivers)
  • NBA players 1.0–4.6 L sweat over a 40-min game
  • Risk factors Equipment, larger body size, hot/humid environments, altitude, diuretics/laxatives
Topic 09 — Fluid and Electrolytes

Assessing Hydration

  • Body weight Weigh before/after exercise → 2%+ loss = inadequate fluid replacement
  • Sweat rate Pre-weight − post-weight + fluid intake − urine produced
  • USG Easy/portable but reflects chronic, not acute, hydration status
  • Urine color Unreliable — beets, B vitamins, food dyes, medications distort it
Topic 09 — Fluid and Electrolytes

Electrolytes & Hyponatremia

Major electrolytes lost in sweat: sodium chloride > potassium > magnesium > calcium.
  • Sodium Highly variable losses (0.2–12.5+ g/L) — helps retain fluid
  • Hyponatremia Blood sodium <130 mmol/L → headache, nausea, cramps
  • Severe (<120 mmol/L) Seizures, cerebral edema, risk of death
Avoid by not drinking more than sweat losses + consuming sodium through food/sport drinks.
Topic 09 — Fluid and Electrolytes

Guidelines: Before & During

  • Before Prehydrate several hours ahead to allow absorption + urine output
  • During Individualize by measuring weight changes across sessions/conditions
  • Sport drink (IOM) 20–30 mEq sodium/L, 2–5 mEq potassium/L, 5–10% carbohydrate
  • Serve Cool — 10–15°C (50–59°F), not cold
Topic 09 — Fluid and Electrolytes

Children & Adolescents

  • Children (40 kg) 5 oz (148 mL) cold water/flavored-salted beverage every 20 min
  • Adolescents (60 kg) 9 oz (266 mL) every 20 min — even without thirst
  • Flavored/salted 15–20 mmol/L NaCl → ↑ voluntary hydration by 90% vs. plain water
Topic 09 — Fluid and Electrolytes

Guidelines: After Activity

Normal meals/snacks with sodium + water restore most fluid/electrolyte losses.
  • Significant dehydration or <12 hr until next session → more aggressive approach
  • Formula ~1.5 L fluid per kg body weight lost (0.7 L per lb) — accounts for ↑ urine from large fluid volumes
Topic 09 — Fluid and Electrolytes

Key Takeaway

Fluid needs are highly individual — build a hydration plan around each athlete's sweat rate, replace sodium losses, and watch for hyponatremia when fluid intake outpaces sweat loss.
